name: Ivan Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI companies, employers, unions, parties and government, and we don't sell or campaign. Everything here is confidential, including the part you'd keep to yourself. What does an ordinary day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage five people who allocate rooms for conferences at a large hotel group. We hold blocks of rooms, adjust the price when bookings change and answer organisers who need twenty rooms after they booked ten. I took this manager post in April. I know the front desk well, but I still muddle the forecast when two events overlap, and my deputy catches it.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what does home look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a whole choir under one roof when their train is late. I have a bachelor's degree, use an AI tool now and then for a first forecast after my deputy has checked it, and I do not trust it on its own. I'm 43, married to Nadia, who is a school science technician, with children aged seven and thirteen and a mortgage. The on-call allowance puts me at the high end of manager pay, we have ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of other hotels nearby. I fix family bicycles on Sundays, which is how I clear my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little automatic filing and a draft forecast would be familiar. Organisers still ring when the choir needs ground-floor rooms, and I can help with that. Our mortgage is covered and the ten-month reserve makes a poor booking month bearable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my team to keep checking the room block against the actual guest list. I'd tell Nadia we can carry on as we do. I wouldn't claim the forecast tool can hear an organiser whose parent cannot climb stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm comfortable, though I'd like to stop making silly overlaps on the calendar. The on-call allowance is good, Nadia's school wage is regular and there are other hotel offices nearby. I can afford to learn this job properly without a rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting next week I'd ask my deputy to check the two largest room blocks with me before I quote a price. Through the first year of a plateau I'd keep the same rota and use the existing forecast tool only for a first pass. I'd put 150 monthly from the allowance into the children's school-trip account while our mortgage and reserve stay covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about wages, and a little sheepish about asking my deputy to check me again. I'd rather be corrected than split another family between hotels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when you split a booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A family of six ended up with three rooms uphill from the conference hotel. I drove their bags over, but the father was wet and angry. A room block has legs attached to it, not just a total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you call that a failure of AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, it was my calendar mistake. The tool showed the two buildings; I read too quickly. I won't blame a machine for a human error just because it sounds modern.

say: I'd tell my team to check **room blocks** against the guest list.
I'd tell Nadia a forecast tool cannot hear an **organiser's access needs**.
think: I'm **comfortable**, though I want to stop making calendar overlaps.
My **on-call allowance**, Nadia's regular wage and nearby hotel offices let me learn without rushing.
do: Check **two large room blocks** with my deputy before quoting prices.
Keep the **existing forecast tool** as a first pass.
Put **150 monthly** into school-trip savings while mortgage and reserve stay covered.
feel: I feel **calm** about wages and sheepish about needing corrections.
S0.quote: I won't blame a machine for a human error just because it sounds modern.
fieldNote: He accepts **responsibility** for a booking error rather than blaming the existing tool.
High pay and a **ten-month reserve** let him learn without immediate income fear.
The school-trip transfer stays behind **mortgage and reserve needs**.

steps.text: Check the two largest room blocks with his deputy before quoting
Put 150 monthly into school-trip savings while mortgage and reserve stay covered

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Writing offers, checking rooms, setting prices, booking and answering organisers are nearly all of our office work. Stronger software could leave one person watching several hotels while porters still carry bags. I am the newest manager and not the quickest with the forecast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell staff to test the new system on awkward access requests, not only tidy bookings. I'd tell organisers there must be a person to call when a room block is wrong. I wouldn't promise our current headcount will hold if the tool works.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could be one of the managers cut. The reserve would keep our mortgage paid for months and Nadia's wage covers some costs, so I can look for another post. But hotel offices nearby may also be hiring fewer people, which makes the number of signs outside misleading.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'd ask for a four-week trial on past conference bookings and learn the new room rules with my deputy on paid time. If the director approves, I'd automate routine confirmation emails while keeping a clerk on access and split-building cases. I'd check actual posted manager vacancies at three nearby hotels before changing jobs, and I'd keep my current salary until a signed offer arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own role, though I have money to search. I want the trial to work, and I also want my deputy to have work next year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a failed access booking?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a guest who asked for a ground-floor room is assigned upstairs, the trial fails that case even if the room is cheap. I'd record the request and the actual room. A good average cannot carry a wheelchair up stairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if your deputy is better at the tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask her to run that part of the trial and write down what she finds. It might make her the better choice to keep, and I have to admit that. I'd still ask the director to be honest with both of us about posts.

say: I'd ask staff to test **access requests** as well as tidy bookings.
I'd tell organisers they need a **person to call** when room blocks fail.
think: My **new manager post** could be cut, even with a strong household buffer.
Nearby hotels may have **fewer actual vacancies** than their signs suggest.
do: Learn **new room rules** with my deputy during a paid four-week trial.
Automate **routine confirmation emails** only if the director approves.
Check **three hotels' posted roles** before leaving my current salary.
feel: I feel **anxious** for my post and my deputy's work.
S1.quote: A good average cannot carry a wheelchair up stairs.
fieldNote: He would share **tool authority** with his deputy even though she might outshine him.
He protects **access and split-building requests** from an automatic confirmation rule.
His cash buffer allows a search, but he counts **posted jobs**, not nearby hotel signs.

steps.text: Learn the new room rules with his deputy during a paid trial
Automate routine confirmation emails only if the director approves
Check posted jobs at three nearby hotels before leaving current pay

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If full AGI can plan and negotiate any room block by 2028, most of my desk could be gone then. Robots carrying bags come around 2031, but a porter job is not waiting for me simply because I know the lobby. I would be looking for an income outside conference booking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team the 2028 date and ask for a written staffing plan. I'd tell Nadia that ten months saved gives us room to test another path, but not room to throw away her pay. I would say publicly that any redeployment offer should name the wage and the actual vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my role could disappear, though I don't know which manager the group would keep. Nadia's regular school wage and our ten-month reserve mean the mortgage would be paid while I search. The hotel jobs around us may change together, so I cannot treat a nearby employer as a safe fallback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this month I'd use my existing tools to offer bicycle brake and tyre repairs to neighbours on two Saturdays, charging only if they accept the work. I'd ask one local bike shop for a paid trial shift and its wage before considering a change, then work it with a mechanic if offered and if Nadia covers pickup for our seven-year-old. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my desk role ends, I'd take a posted workshop job only if its wage plus Nadia's covers mortgage, food and school costs; otherwise I'd keep repairs small while using our reserve to search paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, not lost. The ten-month reserve buys a search. A bicycle hobby does not pay a mortgage by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you repaired someone else's bike for money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not yet. I've fixed our children's brakes and a neighbour's flat tyre for free. I know enough to start small, but I'd want a shop mechanic to check any repair a stranger will ride on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the workshop job last beyond 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hands-on work might, but bookings and parts ordering could change in 2028 and robots arrive around 2031. I can't say a shop will hire me or keep me. I'd only count wages written in an offer, not the bikes in its window.

say: I'd ask for a **written staffing plan** before the booking desk changes in 2028.
I'd tell Nadia any redeployment must have **real wages** and a vacancy.
think: My **manager role could vanish**, though the group might keep one person.
Nadia's wage and **ten months saved** cover the mortgage while I search.
do: Offer **Saturday bike repairs** on two dates using owned tools, charging only for agreed work.
Ask a **bike shop** for a paid trial and confirm seven-year-old pickup.
Take a **posted workshop job** after 2028 only if combined pay covers family bills.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with cash for a search but no proven repair wage.
S2.quote: A bicycle hobby does not pay a mortgage by itself.
fieldNote: He expects **booking decisions in 2028** to change before robots carry bags around 2031.
The bike idea begins with **two repair offers**, not proven paid customers.
A workshop move depends on **wage and vacancy** plus school pickup, even with savings.

steps.text: Offer bicycle repairs on two Saturdays using owned tools if neighbours agree to pay
Take offered paid bike-shop trial with mechanic oversight only if Nadia covers pickup
Take posted workshop work only if combined pay covers mortgage, food and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me find out whether strangers will pay for careful bike repairs while I still draw a hotel salary. The room desk faces AGI in 2031, and hands-on repair faces robots around 2034. A bike shop is a bridge only if its pay covers our bills and it still needs a person at the bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to use the time to test real paid options, not just collect course certificates. I'd tell Nadia I want to keep our ten-month reserve while we measure repair income. I would not tell the children we're opening a shop before we have customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might earn a second wage from repairs by 2031, but I don't know if enough cyclists will return. I could also stay in hotel work until the deadline and use savings to look carefully. The longer runway matters more than the particular job title.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'd complete a weekend wheel-building course if its fee comes from my on-call allowance after mortgage and school costs; I would practise on my own wheel before taking customer work. I'd reserve two Saturday slots a month for paid repairs if people book them, putting actual receipts into a separate account. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply for a posted workshop mechanic trainee role only if the pay with Nadia's wage covers mortgage, food and school costs; if none exists, I'd use our reserve for a broader paid search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the uncertain demand, but five years gives me space to find out. I can pay the mortgage while learning the wheel properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much would two Saturdays bring in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know yet, and I'd rather measure it than invent a number. A neighbour might pay for a tyre, but that doesn't mean a shop will hand me a full wage. I would write down every receipt and every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the course has no place?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep fixing our own bikes and wait for the next class while I stay employed. I wouldn't call myself a wheel builder from a video. Our children need me at home on some Saturdays too.

I'd tell Nadia we should keep our **ten-month reserve** while measuring repair demand.
think: I might earn **some repair income**, but repeat customers are uncertain.
I might keep hotel wages until 2031 while **searching carefully** for another route.
do: Complete a **weekend wheel course** only if allowance covers its fee after bills.
Offer **two paid Saturdays monthly** only if customers book them.
Apply after 2031 for **posted mechanic training** only if combined wages cover family costs.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about demand, with time to test the work.
S3.quote: A neighbour might pay for a tyre, but that doesn't mean a shop will hand me a full wage.
fieldNote: He prefers **measured receipts** to a made-up income projection from his hobby.
Training fees must come from **allowance after bills**, not the mortgage reserve.
A trainee role requires **a real posting** and affordable wages before he moves.

steps.text: Complete weekend wheel-building course only if allowance covers fee after mortgage and school bills
Offer two paid repair Saturdays monthly only when customers book
Apply for posted bike-shop trainee work only if combined wages cover mortgage, food and school costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In ten years our children will be seventeen and twenty-three, and I will be 53. I could spend years at the hotel, save more and decide whether bike repairs are more than a weekend habit. Full AGI still reaches the booking desk in 2036, with physical repair robots around 2039, so a shop would not be a forever refuge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell managers to keep an honest count of roles as software improves. I'd tell friends a decade gives people with wages and savings a better start than people without them. I would ask the hotel group for paid retraining tied to real openings, not a glossy promise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might have paid down the mortgage enough to take fewer hotel hours before 2036, but I can't assume that today. A small repair trade could give me choices if customers actually pay, and the ten-month reserve stays for living costs. I do not want to bet the house on a store I have not opened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd set a cap of two paid bicycle repairs each month while the children are still at home and log the hours and receipts. I'd direct 300 monthly from the on-call allowance toward mortgage principal only after maintaining ten months of cash and covering school costs. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted part-time shop role only if its wage plus Nadia's covers our bills; if that fails, I'd look at other paid work while robots remain about three years away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly calm. We have a long runway and money to choose, though the repair trade has a deadline too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why cap repairs if they pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I want the time to take my son to his matches now, not buy it back when he is grown. Two repairs teach me whether I like paying customers without swallowing every weekend. I'd raise the cap only after talking with Nadia.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if 300 a month cannot fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would leave the cash reserve intact and pay the normal mortgage amount. A school trip or car repair comes first. I won't call a missed extra mortgage payment a failure.

do: Limit **bike repairs** to two monthly while the children need weekends.
Pay **300 extra monthly** on the mortgage only after cash and school costs, unless car repairs arise.
Take a **posted part-time shop role** after 2036 only if combined wages cover bills.
feel: I feel **mostly calm**, with a long runway and a later robot deadline.
S4.quote: I won't call a missed extra mortgage payment a failure.
fieldNote: His **repair cap** protects time with his son and depends on Nadia's agreement to expand.
Extra mortgage payments are **conditional** on cash and school costs, not a fixed promise.
He recognises **2036 booking exposure** and 2039 robot risk for physical repairs.

steps.text: Offer at most two paid bicycle repairs monthly while children need weekend time
Pay 300 extra monthly on mortgage only after cash and school costs, skipping car-repair months
Take posted part-time bike-shop work after 2036 only if combined wages cover bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My room-allocation desk might be cut before I could make even a small second income from repairs, and other hotels may be doing the same thing. I would need clear notice and a real paid vacancy to judge, plus school pickup cover if I took workshop hours. Ten months saved gives us choices, but not a guarantee that a bike shop can replace my hotel wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the person whose conference room block was split between two buildings. A reservation can be right on a screen and wrong for a family arriving with luggage. I still think about a father carrying three bags up the hill in the rain.

headlineQuote: A reservation can be right on a screen and wrong for a family arriving with luggage.
portrait: Ivan, **43**, recently became a room-allocation manager at a large hotel group and still needs his deputy's help with overlapping forecasts.
His **ten-month reserve** and high pay support a mortgage, Nadia and two school-age children, with many nearby hotel employers.
He uses AI **occasionally after checking it** and repairs family bicycles on Sundays as a practical hobby.
Fast AGI threatens his **booking wage**; he would test paid repairs carefully rather than assume a hobby pays family bills.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his room-allocation wage before paid bicycle work is proven.
whatWouldHelp: **Clear notice** and a real paid vacancy with a wage the family can live on.
**School pickup cover** if he takes workshop hours, confirmed before changing jobs.
